1282.title: The Orthodox way
1282.hook: Metropolitan Kallistos Ware explained Orthodoxy to the West with warmth
1282.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a knotted prayer rope, and speak of prayer as standing before God with the mind in the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Newbigin's return: a missionary comes home and sees his own country with new eyes. Your line was home as mission.

One Saturday in London, a young Englishman raised in the Church of England wanders into an Orthodox church. The service is in a language he can't follow. Incense, candles, icons on every wall, a choir with no reason to stop. Nobody explains anything. And yet, he wrote later, he felt he had come home. He became Kallistos Ware: a monk, a teacher at Oxford, and in time a bishop of the Orthodox Church. He spent his life writing about Orthodoxy for people who had never been inside one, plainly, like a friend showing you around his house. Today's word is one of his book titles.

First, the way, the word that matters in that title. In Acts, before they're called Christians, the first followers of Jesus are people of the way: Saul goes to Damascus hunting for, in the King James words, "any of this way." For Ware, faith was less a set of answers to memorize than a road that changes the walker. Orthodox Christians have a bold word for where it leads: theosis, becoming by grace what God is by nature. Second, the heart. In Orthodox teaching the heart isn't where feelings live. It's the deep center of the whole person, where mind and will and love meet. Proverbs says: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." Ware quoted a Russian bishop, Theophan the Recluse: to pray is to stand before God with the mind in the heart. Not thinking about God from up in the head. Coming down. Third, the prayer that carries people there, the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Orthodox writers trace it to a blind man outside Jericho who shouted, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." They repeat it slowly, often on a prayer rope of knots, until, they say, the prayer starts to pray itself. Fourth, the tone. Ware wrote less like a debater than like a host: here is what we do, here is why we love it, come and see.
screen: `FAITH AS A WAY, NOT A LIST.`
`THE HEART: THE CENTER OF THE PERSON.`
`THE MIND COMES DOWN INTO THE HEART.`

segments.voice: The monks who prayed the Jesus Prayer were called hesychasts, from hesychia, stillness. Say the word once inside and let your attention sink from behind your eyes to the middle of your chest; when your mind climbs back up, bring it down again. If you pray, let the Jesus Prayer ride on your breath; if not, rest in the stillness the word names.
The Orthodox way. Kallistos Ware's picture of faith as a road walked with the mind in the heart, shown to outsiders like a host.
Your line: the way of the heart. A road you walk from the center of yourself. See you tomorrow.

1283.title: The three-mile-an-hour God
1283.hook: Kosuke Koyama: God walks at human pace, the speed of love
1283.howItsDone: Some Christians practice slow walking prayer, on pilgrimage routes, in labyrinths or simply around a neighborhood, and some churches hold walks that retell the Emmaus road.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Orthodox way and a word for stillness, hesychia. Your line was the way of the heart.

A rice field in the north of Thailand. A farmer is up to his shins in mud, behind a water buffalo that moves exactly as fast as a water buffalo wants to move. At the edge of the field stands Kosuke Koyama, a Japanese missionary and teacher. He has come to teach the Bible, his bag full of theology from Europe, and he starts to wonder whether he has been in too much of a hurry. What would the gospel sound like if it started here, in the mud, at the buffalo's pace? That question became a short book with an odd title: today's word.
screen: `A TEACHER WITH A BAG OF BOOKS.`

segments.voice: The book is Three Mile an Hour God. His idea: we walk at about three miles an hour, and so, he says, does God's love. It doesn't arrive by express train. It walks beside you. First, the wilderness. Moses tells Israel, in the King James words: "thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart." Forty years, on foot. Why so long? Koyama's answer: the lesson was trust, and trust can't be rushed. A people learning to depend on God one day of manna at a time. Second, Jesus, walking village to village. On the road to Emmaus, two grieving friends are trudging home when a stranger falls in beside them. Luke says: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." He doesn't fly in with the answer. He walks their road at their pace, listening first. Third, the contrast. Koyama watched a world that prized speed: faster machines, faster results. He didn't call speed evil. He said love has its own speed, and it's slow. You can't love someone at a hundred miles an hour; you have to stop, and look, and walk with them. Fourth, the buffalo again. His farmers didn't need a theology flown in from elsewhere. Koyama tried to start from their life, their soil, their pace. That, he thought, is how God came to us: at walking speed, in the dust of one place.
screen: `WE WALK AT ABOUT THREE MILES AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Take a few steps much slower than usual, heel, sole, toes, or, if you can't walk right now, slow your breath to an unhurried stride. Let your body find the speed of someone who isn't late for anything. If you pray, picture walking beside someone on a dusty road; if not, notice what this speed shows you that a run would miss.
The three-mile-an-hour God. Kosuke Koyama's picture of a love that walks at human pace, through the wilderness and down the Emmaus road.
Your line: the speed of love. Slow on purpose, and right beside you. Until tomorrow.

1284.title: African theology
1284.hook: John Mbiti: I am because we are, and the Christian God was already sought in Africa
1284.howItsDone: In African churches, as elsewhere, Christians pray for their families, neighbors and those who came before them by name, and gather to share both mourning and celebration as a community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kosuke Koyama in the rice fields, and a God who walks. Your line was the speed of love.

Ask who you are, and you'll probably give a name, a job, a town. Now ask it another way: who are you with? John Mbiti grew up in Kenya hearing that question answered the second way. He went abroad to study theology, read the great European books, and came home with a puzzle. Many of those books, as he saw it, started with the lonely individual: I think, I choose, I believe. The villages he knew started with family, with neighbors, with the ancestors and the children not yet born. A person was a thread in a cloth. Mbiti spent his life asking what the gospel sounds like when you start from the cloth.
screen: `A PERSON IS A THREAD IN A CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Mbiti, an Anglican priest and scholar, is one of the voices people mean by African theology. First, his summary of how, as he saw it, many African peoples understand a person: I am, because we are. The community makes the person. It flips the famous European line about thinking and existing. You aren't first a self who then joins a group; you become a self through the people who hold you. Second, the Bible's own picture of that shape. Paul calls the church a body: "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." In Acts, the first believers "continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." The Greek word behind fellowship, koinonia, means sharing in common. Third, God was not a stranger. Mbiti gathered the ways African peoples had long spoken of God: creator, provider, the one who sees. He argued that missionaries didn't carry God into Africa as if God had been absent. The gospel came as an answer to a search already under way. Paul says something close in Athens: God made the nations so "that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him." Fourth, the ordinary day. A faith that starts from we notices who's missing from the table.

Let the people who made you come to mind one at a time, a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor who fed you, a friend from a hard year, and to each say quietly: because you were, I am. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if not, notice how many hands are in your story. Then, if you like, think of someone for whom you are one of those hands.
African theology. In John Mbiti's hands, faith that starts from the we, and a God who was already being sought before any missionary arrived.
Your line: I am because we are. Nobody becomes a self alone. Same time tomorrow.

1285.title: Science and faith
1285.hook: physicist-priest John Polkinghorne saw science and faith as two windows
1285.howItsDone: Some Christians work as scientists and see no conflict between the two; churches differ on how they relate scripture and science, and some hold study groups on the question.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Mbiti and African theology: a person as a thread in a cloth. Your line was I am because we are.

Why is the kettle boiling? One answer: the burner heats the water, the molecules speed up, and it turns to steam. Another: because I'd like a cup of tea. Both are true. Neither cancels the other. John Polkinghorne used that kitchen puzzle. He was a physicist who worked on the tiniest pieces of matter, the particles inside the atom. Then he left his professorship, trained for the ministry, and became an Anglican priest. You met another priest and physicist, Georges Lemaître, back in year three. Today's word is the two things Polkinghorne refused to choose between.

He didn't think science and faith were fighting over the same ground. Picture two windows in one house. His own phrase was binocular vision: two eyes, set a little apart, give depth that one eye can't. First window: science. It asks how. How do stars form? It tests, measures, and changes its mind when the evidence says so. He left research physics, but once ordained he kept writing about science for the rest of his life. Second window: faith. It asks why, and what for. Is there purpose? Is there love behind the light? The psalm looks up at the sky a physicist studies and sees more: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Third, where the windows meet. Polkinghorne was struck that the universe can be understood at all. Mathematics worked out on paper fits the way the world actually behaves. Why should it? For him, that was a clue: a world that makes sense, as if made by a mind. A hint worth following, he said, not a proof. Fourth, humility on both sides. Science says, we don't know yet, let's look. Faith at its best says something similar. Gazing at the night sky, the psalmist asks: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Not an answer. Wonder. Polkinghorne thought a scientist and a believer could share it, and one person could be both.

Pick one thing you can see, a plant, your hand, a cup, and look through the how window: what is it made of, how does it work? Then, slowly, the why window: what is it for, what does it mean to you, is anything in it worth thanking someone for? If you pray, offer that thanks to God; if not, let both views sit side by side.
Science and faith. For John Polkinghorne, two windows on one world: one asks how, the other asks why, and together they give depth.
Your line: two windows. One world, and the depth comes from looking through both. See you tomorrow.

1286.title: Block close: the great conversation
1286.hook: two thousand years of thinkers arguing, praying and adding
1286.howItsDone: Christians read the great thinkers of their tradition in study groups, seminaries and on their own, often keeping a favorite writer for years.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Polkinghorne and the kettle: how it boils, and why. Your line was two windows.

A long table, and the chairs keep filling. At one end, Justin, a teacher in Rome, says the seeds of the Word were scattered everywhere, even among the philosophers. Further down, Augustine confesses to God out loud. Boethius talks with Philosophy in his cell. Anselm tries to think the greatest thing that can be thought. Julian of Norwich, quietly: all shall be well. Luther bangs the table about grace. Pascal mutters about reasons of the heart. Kierkegaard insists on the single person. Bonhoeffer writes questions from prison. At the near end, the newest arrivals: a priest-physicist, a teacher from the rice fields, a scholar from Kenya. Nobody here agrees about everything. Today the block of great thinkers closes with a step back to see the whole table.
screen: `STEP BACK AND SEE THE WHOLE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Some call it the great conversation, centuries long. Four things stand out. First, they argued. Anselm built an argument; others pushed back. Aquinas set out his five ways; Ockham shaved away what he thought wasn't needed. Luther and the Catholic thinkers who answered him disagreed deeply. Second, they prayed. Augustine wrote his Confessions as a long prayer. Dionysius climbed a ladder of names into silence. Simone Weil said attention, at its highest, is prayer. For several of them, thinking about God and talking to God were one act. Third, they added. Nobody started from zero. Newman said doctrine grows, like a seed into a tree. Ware handed on the Orthodox way. Mbiti and Koyama asked what the gospel sounds like in their own soil. The letter to the Hebrews pictures the faithful of the past as a crowd in the stands: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight." Fourth, they never finished. The preacher in Ecclesiastes warned, a little wearily: "of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh." The books kept coming anyway, and so did the conversation. That's the good news of an unfinished table: there's still a chair. Anyone who reads, asks, doubts, prays, or writes in a margin is already taking part.

Let the faces of this block pass by, Augustine, Boethius, Julian, Aquinas, Luther, Pascal, Wesley, Kierkegaard, Bonhoeffer, Weil, Merton, Ware, Koyama, Mbiti, Polkinghorne and the rest, and notice the one whose question is also yours, not the one you think you should choose. Let that one take a seat beside you. If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, just hold their question for a moment.
Block close. The end of the great thinkers: people who argued, prayed and added, around a table that still has room.
Your line: join the conversation. Centuries of voices, and room for one more. And that closes the block.

1287.title: How to read Revelation
1287.hook: apocalypse means unveiling, not catastrophe; its images reveal who really rules
1287.howItsDone: Christians read Revelation in different ways: some churches read it chiefly as a message to its first readers, some as prophecy of the end, and some as a picture for every age; its hymns are sung in worship across churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great thinkers' long, unfinished table. Your line was join the conversation.

Zombies in the streets. Cities underwater. A lone survivor with a dog and a shotgun. When a movie poster says apocalypse, it's selling the end of everything. Yet the Bible's last book, which some call the Apocalypse, begins with a blessing, a greeting, grace and peace. There are strange beasts in it, yes: fire, trumpets, a dragon. But it isn't mainly about how the world ends. It's about what's really going on underneath. Back on Mark's little apocalypse, you heard that Christians read the end-time pictures in several ways. This path now reads it slowly, starting with the word on its front door.
screen: `A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH GRACE AND PEACE.`

segments.voice: In Greek, the book's very first word is apokalypsis: an uncovering, an unveiling, the cloth pulled off something that was there all along. The King James puts it: "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass." A revelation, not a catastrophe. Second, what gets unveiled. John writes to churches, some under pressure, in a world where other powers looked like they owned everything. Revelation pulls back the curtain on another throne, in heaven, and the one who actually rules. One scene holds the key. John sees a sealed scroll and weeps, because no one can open it. An elder tells him: "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book." John turns to see the lion, and sees "a Lamb as it had been slain." A lion announced; a wounded lamb appears. Some readers see the whole book in that turn: for them, power, unveiled, looks like self-giving love. Third, how Christians read it. Some mainly as a letter to churches in John's own day. Some as largely about the end of history. Some as a picture of every age. Churches weigh these readings differently, and some readers combine them. Fourth, the tone. Many readers find that, read slowly, it sounds like courage, not panic. Near its end it promises: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." That's where the unveiling is headed.

Let one line from the opening sit with you: "Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy." The book blesses whoever reads it, so if strange images or old fears about the end come up, let them pass like weather. If you pray, ask to see what's really there; if not, rest in the idea that something true might lie under the surface of today.
Apocalypse. From the Greek apokalypsis, an uncovering. Not the end of the world: the cloth pulled off, to show who really rules.
Your line: an unveiling. A word to open the book with, not to fear. Rest well.

1288.howItsDone: The Greek letters alpha and omega appear on Christian altars, candles and vestments; in some churches the Easter candle is marked with them as a sign that Christ is the beginning and the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word on Revelation's front door: apocalypse, the cloth pulled off. Your line was an unveiling.

From: John. To: the seven churches which are in Asia. Before any dragon or trumpet, Revelation reads like mail: who it's from, who it's to. Then the greeting, ordinary and not ordinary at all: "Grace be unto you, and peace, from him which is, and which was, and which is to come." These are real congregations in real cities, each with a name you'll meet soon. And the letter opens by naming God in a strange order. Today, the first eight verses, ending at a pair of letters.

First, the order. You'd expect: who was, who is, who will be. John writes: who is, who was, who is to come. He starts with now. Some readers hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush, I AM. Before God is a memory or a hope, God is present, today. Second, Jesus, in three titles. The letter sends grace "from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth." A witness who told the truth, even to death. The firstborn from the dead. A ruler over the rulers. For churches under pressure, that last title would land. Third, a sudden song. John can't finish his greeting without breaking into praise: "Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood." Praise breaks into the middle of the mail. Fourth, the signature. God speaks in the first person: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty." Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, like saying A to Z. Every word, every story, sits between them. The claim isn't only that God was there at the start and will be at the finish. God holds the whole alphabet, including the messy middle where the seven churches were living, and where everybody lives.

segments.voice: Hold the first thing you did today and the last thing you expect to do tonight like bookends, and let everything in between come gently into view: the conversations, the work, the worry, the small good things. If you pray, say quietly, I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, and rest your whole day between those letters; if not, just let the day be held, start to finish, for a moment.
Alpha and Omega. The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and Revelation's name for the one who holds everything from A to Z.
